claims.text: Conventional polycrystalline copper has an FCC crystal structure.
Refining the grain structure of polycrystalline copper enhances its ductility at ambient conditions.
The FCC structure of copper provides multiple slip systems.
Multiple FCC slip systems enable efficient dislocation motion in copper.
Thermomechanical processing can produce controlled grain refinement in copper.
Thermomechanical processing can optimize the stacking-fault energy of copper.
Grain-size reduction in copper minimizes stress concentrations.
Grain-size reduction facilitates uniform dislocation glide on the FCC slip systems of copper.
Combining grain refinement with the FCC structure reduces barriers to dislocation movement in copper.
Improved dislocation transmission and relief of stress concentrations can delay premature localization or cracking and promote tensile ductility.
Grain-refined copper will have higher uniform elongation than coarse-grained copper at room temperature.
Grain-refined copper will have improved overall ductility relative to coarse-grained copper.
The proposed ductility improvement will occur without a significant loss in strength.
Temperature changes can alter stacking-fault-mediated deformation behavior and thereby change the proposed ductility response.
At very high strain rates, deformation mechanisms other than the proposed uniform dislocation glide may dominate.
The quantitative ductility improvement depends on the achieved grain size and processing conditions.
The quantitative ductility improvement depends on the modification of stacking-fault energy.
Failure of refined-grain samples to show a statistically significant ductility improvement over identically tested coarse-grained controls would falsify the hypothesis.
